svg.aria-label: Diagram: Microsoft Entra hybrid identity, separating the synchronization topology decision from the authentication method decision, comparing password hash synchronization, pass-through authentication and federation by which on-premises account states each enforces, the unsupported multi-server topology that nevertheless works, how Cloud Sync differs from Connect Sync, and why password hash synchronization is the recommended backup whatever else is chosen
svg.title: Two independent decisions that everyone conflates: how objects arrive, and how passwords are checked
svg.text: Two decisions, not one: how objects get into the tenant, and how passwords get checked.
“The choice of synchronization technology does not determine or change the authentication behavior for user sign-ins.”
Decision two: what the authentication method actually buys you
METHOD
ON-PREMISES SERVERS NEEDED
ACCOUNT STATES IT ENFORCES
Password hash sync
none beyond the sync server
disabled only, “up to 30-minute delay”
Pass-through auth
one per agent — three recommended
disabled, locked out, expired, password
expired, sign-in hours
Federation (AD FS)
“Two or more AD FS servers, two or
more WAP servers in the perimeter”
all of the above, plus sAMAccountName
sign-in and third-party MFA
That first row is the real trade. Password hash sync is the simplest thing that works and the only one that cannot tell you a
password has expired or an account is locked. It also has a quiet trap: set “user must change password at next logon” and
“the password hash will not be synced to Microsoft Entra ID” until the user actually changes it.
The topology that is unsupported and works
Two Connect Sync servers to one tenant is “unsupported
even if these servers are configured to synchronize with a
mutually exclusive set of objects”. Then, in brackets:
“(While not supported, this still works.)”
Nothing errors. Nothing warns. It runs until the day you
need support, or the two servers disagree.
The one permitted second server is a staging server.
Cloud Sync moves the orchestration off-site
Connect Sync: one server holds the configuration, the
rules and the state. It is the single point of failure.
Cloud Sync: lightweight agents, outbound only, over
Service Bus, speaking SCIM. Config lives in the tenant.
Multiple active agents with automatic failover, and it
natively handles disconnected forests — the merger case
Connect Sync cannot reach without joining them first.
“Microsoft’s strategic direction for hybrid identity.”
Turn password hash sync on whatever else you choose — and the reason is an outage story
Microsoft describes two kinds of organisation it has helped after a ransomware attack took their on-premises servers down:
Had password hash sync already on
switched primary method, “back online in a matter of hours”
Had not
“resort[ed] to untrusted external consumer email systems”; weeks
Two caveats worth knowing before relying on it: the failover is manual — “you must use Microsoft Entra Connect to switch the
sign-on method manually” — and it only helps if it was “configured before the failure event”.
And ID Protection needs it regardless of how you sign in
“Microsoft Entra ID Protection requires Password Hash Sync regardless of which sign-in method you choose, to provide the
Users with leaked credentials report.” So post #48’s highest-confidence detection is off in a federated tenant without it.
What sync discards without telling you
Two enabled accounts, or two mailboxes
“the sync engine picks one and ignores the other”
A linked mailbox with no active account
not exported, and “not represented as a member in any group”
Duplicate groups across forests
“aren’t consolidated with the default configuration” — users are
Sources: Microsoft Entra Connect supported topologies, Authentication for Microsoft Entra hybrid identity solutions, and What is Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync, on Microsoft Learn.
